title: BCS theory: the weak-coupling baseline
summary: Cooper pairing, the gap equation and the 3.528 gap ratio, with the assumptions that make these useful model benchmarks rather than universal material rules.

review.scope: Edited adaptation of the pinned B1 chapter with selected primary passages of Cooper (1956) and Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (1957), plus model-equation and notation checks.
limitations: This is a scoped theoretical review, not a full scientific validation or independent reproduction of every derivation.
No sample-specific experimental values or pairing mechanisms have been verified for this entry.
Josephson, flux quantization and microscopic GL derivations mentioned in the pinned chapter are not independently reviewed here.
The one-spin density of states, weak-coupling and phase-coherence assumptions must not be discarded when reusing formulas.

claims.statement: BCS theory provides a microscopic pairing framework and a useful weak-coupling reference point. This article concerns its equilibrium, single-band, isotropic implementation with a smooth density of states and an effective attraction near the Fermi surface. Those assumptions define a model, not a classification of every superconductor. Agreement with one numerical ratio does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction.
claims.conditions: Equilibrium isotropic single-band model, weak net attraction in an energy shell, smooth one-spin DOS and sufficient phase coherence; a two-electron Cooper problem is not the full many-body solution.

claims.statement: The Cooper problem asks what happens when two electrons interact above an otherwise inert, filled Fermi sea. In the idealized attractive-shell model, a bound pair exists below the two-particle continuum for arbitrarily weak net attraction. The filled sea and its excluded states are essential to this result. It is not a claim that every attractive potential binds two isolated electrons in vacuum, nor is the two-electron calculation alone a construction of the finite-density superconducting state.

claims.statement: The general pairing construction should not be equated with a universal weak-coupling phonon mechanism. A frequency-dependent interaction, several coupled bands, an anisotropic gap or a rapidly varying density of states requires a more suitable equation. Phase fluctuations can also separate a pairing scale from the temperature at which long-range or quasi-long-range coherence develops. The simple gap equation above does not calculate that fluctuation problem.

claims.statement: The familiar isotope exponent $-d\ln T_c/d\ln M=1/2$ follows only if the cutoff has harmonic mass scaling and the remaining effective parameters are mass-independent. Changes in structure or coupling invalidate that inference. Likewise, a nonstandard gap ratio can motivate tests of stronger coupling or anisotropy; it does not, by itself, prove a named alternative mechanism. These applicability cautions follow the scope of the pinned B1 source chapter and are not new experimental findings.

claims.statement: Use BCS as a controlled baseline: define the band model, interaction window and normalization before fitting. Check that the inferred scales fit within the regime assumed by the calculation, rather than extrapolating an exponential formula into a flat-band or low-density regime. Compare alternative explanations using measurements that distinguish them. In particular, finding a Cooper instability is a starting point for a many-body theory, not the final demonstration of a material's phase coherence or pairing mediator.
